source.title: Scaling Behavior Cloning Improves Causal Reasoning: An Open Model for Real-Time Video Game Playing
source.authors: Yuguang Yue; Irakli Salia; Samuel Hunt; Chris Green; Wenzhe Shi; Jonathan J. Hunt

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling-law analysis to behavior-cloning game policies and reports test-loss curves over model sizes and training-data sizes; it does not study language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study measures behavior-cloning test loss (using keyboard perplexity as the test loss) across model sizes and training-frame quantities. It does not test language-model loss scaling, small-run extrapolation to much larger runs, or a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Numeric test-loss points for most curves are available only in figures. The separate causality-score findings are recorded as related but not covered by the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits a Kaplan-style power law L(D)=L∞+(Dc/D)^α to behavior-cloning test loss (keyboard perplexity) across five dataset sizes and four model sizes. This is a new setting (video-game policies, multi-epoch data-constrained training) with its own result on whether the power-law form holds beyond text pretraining.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors conclude that test loss follows a power law in dataset size and that larger models achieve lower test loss in data-abundant regimes. Their headline conclusion, which the record omits, is that scaling model and data size raises causality scores, suggesting scale as a remedy for causal confusion in behavior cloning.
record.recipe_differences: This is a behavior-cloning policy study, not a neural language-model pretraining scaling-law study; it varies model size and training frames but does not test token/compute scaling or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported causality-score ordering depends on checkpoint selection: selecting the lowest-test-loss checkpoint gives trends different from some intermediate training-step comparisons. The causality score also has an exception in extremely data-limited regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: Online game scores improve only weakly with model size. On Simple-FPS, 150M scores 25.3±6.5 and 1.2B scores 26.6±3.7, within one SD. Separately, a pretrained 600M model reaches much lower test loss but is not preferred in human evaluation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In behavior-cloning game policies, lower test loss and larger scale do not reliably translate into better online task performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Causality scores rise with model size, data size and training, except at 30M frames and at some intermediate checkpoints.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In behavior-cloning game policies, greater model capacity and more unique training frames generally increase measured dependence on visual inputs.

record.problems: Most test-loss values and curves are presented only in figures; the text supplies fit parameters for the 1.2B model but not numerical loss points for the other model sizes. The study tests one behavior-cloning game-policy setup, not language-model pretraining.

untested.parts: Power law in parameters or compute: no model-size fit, only four sizes compared qualitatively. Data scaling over several orders of magnitude: about 16x only. Image or video generative models, fine-tuning and transfer laws.
No extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
No fixed-parameter shape comparison. Depth and width vary across sizes but are not analysed.

missing.what: Test loss versus model size within each dataset fraction: larger models are lower in data-abundant fractions but not in small-data fractions.
Pretraining on IDM-pseudo-labelled unlabelled video, then fine-tuning: lower test loss at the same frame count for 600M.
Downstream game scores by model size (Table 1) and human preference results (Fig. 4a).

record.verdict_notes: Only a data-size law is fitted. It spans about 1.2 orders of magnitude and is computed in a repeated-data (multi-epoch) regime, using the best checkpoint. The V5 support is therefore narrow. Learning rates and batch sizes differ by model size (Table 2). The 600M model has only 9 layers versus 20 for the 300M model, so model-size comparisons are confounded by shape.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss of language models as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether fits on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities and regimes beyond this behavior-cloning game-policy setting, including repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer.
Predictability of downstream task performance from language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Whether exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with setup or fitting choices, or curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: P2P 1.2B
rows.operation_detail: Fit test loss against training-frame count across dataset sizes.

conditions.value: Keyboard perplexity used as test loss

rows.measure: Test loss versus number of training frames
rows.note: The text reports these fit estimates for the 1.2B model and describes the fit as close. It does not provide numeric loss values for the individual dataset sizes in the text.
rows.check: Linkage and state are fine. The fitted data range is only about 30M–500M frames (6%–100%), roughly 1.2 orders of magnitude. Each point is the lowest test loss over multiple epochs (repeated data), not a single-pass run. Only a data-size law is fitted; no parameter or compute law is fitted.

rows.subject: P2P models across the tested model and dataset sizes (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measure causality score across model sizes, dataset sizes, and training steps.

conditions.value: Causality scores evaluated across model and dataset sizes

rows.measure: Causality score based on KL divergence between predictions for original and image-perturbed inputs
rows.value: Authors report that scores generally increase with model size, dataset size, and training; increase with unique frames except in extremely data-limited regimes.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation on the order of 10−4
rows.note: This is a related causal-behavior result, not a test of the loss, extrapolation, or allocation outcomes named in the claim versions. The authors note a low-data exception and that intermediate training checkpoints can reverse the dataset-size ranking.
rows.check: The causality score is a different construct from loss scaling, so it is correctly unlinked.

relationships.condition: P2P behavior-cloning game policies, 150M–1.2B params, multi-epoch training on 30M–500M frames, test loss = keyboard perplexity
relationships.reason: Test loss versus dataset size fits a power law closely for all four model sizes: L∞=1.111, α=0.2336 for 1.2B (R1–R4).
relationships.display_finding: Dataset-size power laws closely fitted test loss for all four model sizes, with L∞=1.111 and α=0.2336 for the 1.2B model.

relationships.condition: Model-size dimension in low-data regimes (6–12% of data)
relationships.reason: Authors state larger models achieve lower loss only when the dataset is relatively large (App. D.6, Fig. 14). This is text-based; no row records it.
relationships.display_finding: Larger models achieved lower loss only when datasets were relatively large, leaving the size advantage absent in the low-data regime.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
